title: The Fire-Master of Colour: Süderen-Linden to Zürich
register: national mythology, the canon is true

stops.name: Süderen-Linden, the birth-house in the Bernese Oberland
stops.campa: Johannes Itten is born on 11 November in Süderen-Linden, a scatter of farms in the folds of the Bernese hills, where the Emmental leans toward the high Oberland. He is a farmer's and schoolmaster's child, reared among cattle, meadows and the strict Protestant year. The seasons here teach the first lesson he will preach all his life: that everything living moves by rhythm and contrast: light against dark, warmth against cold, the breath drawn in and let go. The mountains stand over him like coloured walls at dawn.
suggested_refs: Süderen-Linden hamlet, municipality of Linden BE

stops.name: Thun, the uncle's house on the Aare
stops.campa: His father dies in 1892 and the family moves often, but the boy is rooted again at ten, sent to live with his uncle in Thun where the Aare runs green-blue out of the lake beneath the castle. Here he attends the secondary school and first feels the pull between the ordered discipline of Swiss teaching and the wilder image-world waking in him. Thun is the town of his youth; to it his art will return in old age, and its museum will one day hold his colours.

stops.name: Hofwil, the teacher-training college near Bern
stops.campa: From 1904 to 1908 Itten trains as an elementary schoolmaster at the seminary of Hofwil, in the reform tradition of Pestalozzi and Fellenberg. He absorbs the kindergarten method of Friedrich Fröbel: the gifts, the folded papers, the primary forms and colours given to a child's hand before words. This is the seed of the Vorkurs a decade before the Bauhaus exists: that art, like reading, has an alphabet, and that the hand and the whole body must be schooled together with the eye.

stops.name: Schwarzenburg, the village schoolmaster
stops.campa: Newly qualified, Itten takes a post as village schoolmaster in the Bernese countryside around Schwarzenburg, teaching by Fröbel's principles. But the classroom cannot hold him. He tries the mathematics and sciences at university in Bern, then turns wholly toward art. The schoolmaster who leaves the school never truly leaves teaching: he will spend his life making pupils, only now in painting and in colour. The Swiss discipline goes with him like a second skeleton.

stops.name: Geneva, the École des Beaux-Arts and Eugène Gilliard
stops.campa: Itten comes to Geneva and the École des Beaux-Arts, and above all to the painter Eugène Gilliard, who teaches an analytic geometry of the picture: the diagonal, the circle, the taut construction beneath appearance. Here Itten learns that a composition can be read like a skeleton x-rayed out of the flesh. He will carry Gilliard's method into every school he founds. Twice he crosses French Switzerland to this training; the second time it takes hold and sends him, hungry, toward Germany and the new painting.

stops.name: Stuttgart, the Academy and the masterclass of Adolf Hölzel
stops.campa: In 1913 Itten enters the Academy of Fine Arts in Stuttgart and finds his true master: Adolf Hölzel, prophet of abstraction and of colour law. In 1914 he is taken into Hölzel's celebrated masterclass. From Hölzel comes the doctrine that will become Itten's own gospel: the theory of contrasts, the ordered scale of hues, the conviction that colour obeys laws as music obeys harmony. Among his fellows are Oskar Schlemmer, Willi Baumeister, Ida Kerkovius and Hermann Stenner; here Itten paints his first pure abstractions.
suggested_refs: Adolf Hölzel, colour and contrast theory

stops.name: Stuttgart, the first pupils and the turn to teaching
stops.campa: In 1916, on Hölzel's own recommendation, Itten begins to give private drawing lessons in Stuttgart. He discovers that teaching is his real medium: he watches how a hand tightens, how breath falters, how fear freezes the line, and he begins to devise exercises to unbind them. A pupil, Agathe Mark, urges him east. It is at Stuttgart too that Itten first tests the Mazdaznan practices of breath and rhythm on his students. The discipline that will scandalise Weimar was rehearsed here in quiet.

stops.name: Vienna, the private art school
stops.campa: Itten opens his own art school in Vienna in the autumn of 1916 and from private lessons builds a class. Here his method crystallises: every session begins with exercises of concentration, breathing and rhythm before the pupil is allowed to draw. He teaches the analysis of Old Masters, the study of natural forms (a thistle, a spray of grasses) and the contrasts of texture and colour. Pupils he forms in Vienna, among them a devoted circle, will follow him to Weimar and staff the Bauhaus preliminary course.
suggested_refs: the Viennese Itten-pupils at the Bauhaus

stops.name: Vienna, the embrace of Mazdaznan
stops.campa: In Vienna Itten gives himself wholly to Mazdaznan, the neo-Zoroastrian fire-faith of Otoman Zar-Adusht Ha'nish, born Otto Hanisch: a doctrine of conscious breathing, fasting, vegetarian diet, cleansing and rhythmic exercise, promising to restore the Earth to a garden where man may again converse with God. Zarathustra's ancient religion of light and purity is reborn as a modern discipline of the body. Itten reads it as the key that binds his art to a cosmos: colour is light, light is fire, and the fire must be tended in the breathing artist himself.

stops.name: Vienna, Alma Mahler's circle and the call from Gropius
stops.campa: Itten moves in Vienna's avant-garde salon (Alma Mahler, Adolf Loos, the shadow of Klimt and Kokoschka) and marries his former pupil Hildegard Anbelang. It is Alma Mahler who speaks his name to Walter Gropius, newly founding a school in Weimar that would weld all the arts into one building, one craft, one new man. Gropius calls him. Itten will bring not only a method but a faith, and the collision of the two, the engineer's Bauhaus and the fire-priest's, is already written into the invitation.

stops.name: Weimar, arrival at the Staatliches Bauhaus
stops.campa: In October 1919 Itten arrives at the newly proclaimed Staatliches Bauhaus as one of its first Masters of Form, called by Gropius the year of founding. Into a school still improvising itself he brings a fully formed pedagogy and a fully formed cult. He is the first of the painter-masters; soon he will draw in Paul Klee and Georg Muche after him. From the beginning he is the Bauhaus's most magnetic and most disturbing presence: the man who teaches art as a spiritual askesis.
suggested_refs: Bauhaus Weimar, main building (Van de Velde)

stops.name: Weimar, the Vorkurs, the preliminary course
stops.campa: Itten creates the Vorkurs, the preliminary course every Bauhaus student must pass: the invention that remakes art education across the century. He unlearns the academy. Students knead materials to feel their texture; they draw the rhythm of a storm, the structure of a thistle; they build contrast-studies of rough and smooth, light and dark. The exercises begin with the body loosened and the breath ordered. From this half-year the pupil is reborn, freed of dead convention, and only then sent into the workshops.
stops.quote: Everyone is creative and this creativity must be freed... The teacher must awaken it and let it grow according to its own inner law.
stops.quote_source: Johannes Itten, on the aim of the preliminary course (Mein Vorkurs am Bauhaus / Design and Form)
suggested_refs: 'Design and Form: The Basic Course at the Bauhaus'

stops.name: Weimar, the Tempelherrenhaus studio
stops.campa: Itten's studio is the Tempelherrenhaus, the neo-Gothic garden pavilion in the Park an der Ilm, and around it his cult gathers. Before his office rises his Tower of Fire: a spiralling glass-and-form sculpture of 1920 climbing toward the sky, marrying architecture, colour, mathematics and music into one Gesamtkunstwerk, the Bauhaus idea made an idol. In 1920 his son Matthias is born and he paints the tender 'Kinderbild'. The master is at his zenith, half teacher, half hierophant.
suggested_refs: Tempelherrenhaus, Park an der Ilm, Weimar
Johannes Itten, 'Tower of Fire' (Turm des Feuers, 1920)

stops.name: Weimar, the colour sphere and the seven contrasts
stops.campa: At the Bauhaus Itten sets down the discipline of colour that will be his monument: the colour sphere and twelve-part wheel, and above all the seven contrasts: hue, light-dark, cold-warm, complementary, simultaneous, saturation, and extension. He teaches that each pupil carries a subjective chord of colours, a personal timbre to be discovered and honoured, alongside the objective laws. Colour, to him, is no decoration but the living speech of light itself, and the artist a tuner of its intervals.
stops.quote: Color is life; for a world without colors appears to us as dead. Colors are primordial ideas, the children of light.
stops.quote_source: Johannes Itten, The Art of Color (Kunst der Farbe, 1961)

stops.name: Weimar, the Mazdaznan community of the Bauhaus
stops.campa: From 1919 to 1923 Itten and Georg Muche keep a Mazdaznan community inside the Bauhaus, a secular monastery of some twenty devoted students. They shave their heads and wear the pseudo-priestly cloak; they fast on fixed days, sing harmony-exercises with rhythmic movement, take purges and enemas, eat a mash so laden with garlic that visitors reel from the studios. Before the pencil touches paper, the master leads them in breathing. Art here is not made but purified out of the cleansed and quickened body.
suggested_refs: photographs of Itten in the Mazdaznan robe, shaved head

stops.name: Weimar, the garlic vote and the war of two Bauhäuser
stops.campa: In December 1921 the Bauhaus kitchen becomes a battlefield of the spirit: a vote is held over whether onion and garlic shall rule the common table. Itten's fasting fire-monks against Gropius's vision of a school geared to the machine and the modern world. The two Bauhäuser can no longer share one roof. Gropius, courting industry and the new objectivity, sees the cult as a private religion strangling the school; Itten sees the workshops surrendering the soul to the engine.

stops.name: Weimar, the break with Gropius
stops.campa: The rupture comes. Gropius turns the Bauhaus toward 'Art and Technology: A New Unity' and calls in the Constructivist Moholy-Nagy; there is no place for the fire-priest. Itten gives notice and departs in 1923, his preliminary course to be inherited and stripped of its ritual by Moholy-Nagy and then by Josef Albers. The Vorkurs survives him and conquers the schools of the world; the incense and the breathing do not. He leaves as a founder cast out of his own founding, carrying the fire homeward to Switzerland.
suggested_refs: Moholy-Nagy succeeds Itten in the Vorkurs
'Art and Technology: A New Unity' (1923 Bauhaus exhibition)

stops.name: Herrliberg, the Aryana community and the Ontos workshops
stops.campa: Itten withdraws to Herrliberg on the Lake of Zürich, to the international Mazdaznan settlement called Aryana, and founds there the Ontos weaving and carpet workshops, bringing the Bauhaus loom-master Gunta Stölzl for a season. On the terraced hillside above the lake he lives the fire-faith undiluted: breathing, fasting, the vegetable garden, the dyed threads. For two years the outcast keeps his temple. But community life sours with quarrels, and in October 1925 he breaks camp again and turns toward Berlin.

stops.name: Berlin, the Itten-Schule
stops.campa: In Berlin Itten founds his own school, the Itten-Schule, which becomes the great private rival of the Bauhaus. He gathers old comrades (Georg Muche, Lucia Moholy, Mordecai Bronstein) and teaches the preliminary course as free art education. In spring 1929 he raises a purpose-built New-Building house at Konstanzer Strasse 14 in Wilmersdorf, roof-terrace for the morning gymnastics. Here his method flowers a second time, in the capital, for the years the Weimar Republic has left.

stops.name: Krefeld, the textile school
stops.campa: Called to the Rhineland, Itten takes the directorship of the Prussian higher textile school at Krefeld, the German silk city, and transforms a trade school into an art college of weaving and cloth. He marries his second wife, Anneliese Schlösser, a weaving teacher and former pupil. He designs and dyes, marries loom and colour theory. Here the textile thread of his life, from Ontos to Krefeld to the Zürich weaving school, twists into a single strand.
suggested_refs: Höhere Fachschule für textile Flächenkunst, Krefeld

stops.name: Munich, condemned as 'Degenerate Art'
stops.campa: The new masters of Germany name his art a sickness. In the summer of 1937 works of Itten hang in the Nazi exhibition of 'Degenerate Art' at Munich, mockery for the crowds. In 1938 Krefeld dismisses him: a foreigner, a Bauhaus man, an enemy of the blood-and-soil order. The fire-faith that once dreamed a purified new man is itself branded impure by a darker cult of purity. The wandering master must wander again, out of Germany altogether.

stops.name: Amsterdam, the exile and the Stedelijk velum
stops.campa: For a season Itten lives in Amsterdam, lecturing and painting in exile, and designs a great cloth velum to hang beneath the glass roof of the Stedelijk Museum's entrance. Then the art historian Sigfried Giedion brings word of a post open in Zürich. Itten applies, and the door of his own country opens. The long expulsion, Weimar, then Berlin, then Krefeld, then Holland, bends at last back toward the Swiss hills where he began.

stops.name: Zürich, director of the Kunstgewerbeschule and Museum
stops.campa: In December 1938 Itten assumes in Zürich the joint directorship of the School of Arts and Crafts (Kunstgewerbeschule) and its Museum of Applied Arts. In 1939 he plants the Vorkurs once more, the preliminary course in form and colour, in the general foundation programme: the third flowering of Weimar's invention, now on neutral Swiss ground while war burns across the border. The exile is home, the method reborn, the ritual quietly laid aside; what remains is the clear discipline of the eye.

stops.name: Zürich, the Textile School
stops.campa: In 1943 Itten adds the directorship of the Zürich Textile School to his offices, gathering again the thread that runs from Ontos through Krefeld. In these Zürich years the wanderer becomes an institution: three schools, a museum, the elder statesman of Swiss design, shaping a generation of makers by the same conviction he carried out of the Emmental: that seeing is a discipline and colour a law that can be taught.

stops.name: Zürich, the Museum Rietberg and the von der Heydt collection
stops.campa: For a decade Itten courts Baron Eduard von der Heydt for his collection of Asian and non-European art, and in 1952 the Museum Rietberg opens in the Wesendonck villa, with Itten as its founding director. The old admirer of Zarathustra and of Eastern breath now enshrines the arts of Asia in a Swiss park. His late years turn eastward again: he takes up Japanese ink, sumi-e, the brushed sign, closing the circle his fire-faith first opened decades before.

stops.name: Zürich, 'The Art of Color' set down at last
stops.campa: In 1961 Itten publishes 'Kunst der Farbe' (The Art of Color), the great codex toward which his whole life has been climbing since Hölzel's masterclass: the colour sphere, the twelve-part wheel, the seven contrasts, the doctrine of subjective timbre. Two years later he sets down 'Mein Vorkurs am Bauhaus', the testament of the preliminary course. The schoolmaster of the Emmental has written the schoolbook of colour for the world. Retired since 1956, he now teaches only through the page.
stops.quote: Color is life, for a world without color seems dead. As a flame produces light, light produces color.
stops.quote_source: Johannes Itten, The Art of Color (Kunst der Farbe, 1961), opening
suggested_refs: Johannes Itten, 'Mein Vorkurs am Bauhaus' / 'Design and Form' (1963)

stops.name: Zürich, the Kunsthaus retrospective and the Venice Biennale
stops.campa: In 1964 the Kunsthaus Zürich mounts a great retrospective of Itten's painting, and in 1966 his work goes to the Venice Biennale: the outcast of Weimar honoured at last as a master painter and not only a legendary teacher. Late abstractions of pure geometric colour, hue laid against hue by the seven laws he found, glow on the walls: the theory made visible, the fire distilled to clear light. The circle of the life is nearly closed.

stops.name: Zürich, death and the grave at Hönggerberg
stops.campa: Johannes Itten dies at Zürich on 25 March 1967, seventy-eight years old, and is laid in the cemetery on the Hönggerberg above the city. The farmer's son of Süderen-Linden ends among the schools and museums of Zürich, having carried the Emmental's rhythm of contrast, Hölzel's colour law and Zarathustra's fire across half a century and half a continent. The Vorkurs he made still opens art education everywhere; The Art of Color still teaches the eye. The fire is banked but not gone out.
